## The question we're answering {.smaller}

::: {.keypoint}
Using a synthetic linked birth cohort: **is 17-hydroxyprogesterone (17-OHP) measured on the
newborn screening dried blood spot associated with gestational age — and do maternal factors
predict preterm birth?**
:::

Three files, exactly the shape of a real linked extract:

| File | Unit | Key | n |
|---|---|---|---|
| `births.csv` | one row per **infant** | `infant_id`, `momid` | 1,239 |
| `mothers.csv` | one row per **mother** | `momid` | 1,200 |
| `screening.csv` | one row per **specimen** | `infant_id` + `specimen_no` | 1,338 |

: {tbl-colwidths="[26,32,28,14]"}

. . .

<p class="small muted">1,239 infants but only 1,200 mothers, and 1,338 specimens for 1,239 infants.
Those two mismatches are the whole lesson of the joins section. Fully synthetic data —
safe to share, safe to paste anywhere.</p>


# The workflow {.section-break}

## Every analysis is the same six steps {.smaller}

<div style="font-size:0.9em; line-height:1.9">
**1 · Import** → get it into R, as the right types<br>
**2 · Tidy** → one row per observation, one column per variable<br>
**3 · Transform** → filter, derive, join, aggregate<br>
**4 · Visualise** → look at it before you model it<br>
**5 · Model** → the part that takes 5% of the time<br>
**6 · Communicate** → tables, figures, a reproducible document
</div>

. . .

::: {.keypoint .smaller}
Steps 1–3 are **80% of the work** and where essentially all the errors live.
A wrong `left_join()` will not throw an error — it will quietly give you a different cohort.
That is why today is mostly steps 1–3.
:::

---

## Import {.smaller}

```r
library(tidyverse)

births    <- read_csv("data/births.csv")       # readr: fast, tells you its guesses
mothers   <- read_csv("data/mothers.csv")
screening <- read_csv("data/screening.csv")

# other formats you will actually meet
readxl::read_excel("lab.xlsx", sheet = "Results")
haven::read_sas("ices_extract.sas7bdat")       # ← SAS datasets, directly
haven::read_dta("nhanes.dta")
```

::: {.cols}
<div>
::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" .smaller}
**`haven::read_sas()` is the bridge.** Your supervisor's `.sas7bdat` opens in R without
SAS installed, formats and labels included. This is how most people move from SAS to R.
:::
</div>
<div>
::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple" .smaller}
`read_csv()` **guesses** column types from the first 1000 rows. If a numeric column has
`"N/A"` at row 4000, you get a character column. Always check `spec()` or `glimpse()`.
:::
</div>
:::

---

## Look before you leap {.smaller}

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| min-lines: 6
glimpse(births)
```

::: {.small .muted}
`glimpse()` is `str()` with better manners: every column, its type, and the first few values,
on one screen.
:::

## …and the problems are already visible {.smaller}

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| min-lines: 8
count(births, sex)                       # four categories for a binary variable
summary(births$ga_weeks)
colSums(is.na(mothers))                  # missingness, per column
n_distinct(screening$infant_id)          # 1205 infants…
nrow(screening)                          # …but 1338 specimen rows
```

. . .

::: {.keypoint .smaller}
Three problems found in four lines: **inconsistent coding**, **missing maternal BMI**,
and **repeat specimens**. Find these now, not after you've written the discussion section.
:::

---

## The pipe: `|>` {.smaller}

The pipe takes the thing on the left and makes it the first argument of the thing on the right.
It turns nested code inside-out so you read it in the order it happens.

::: {.cols}
<div>
### Without
```r
arrange(
  filter(
    select(births, infant_id, ga_weeks, site),
    ga_weeks < 37),
  ga_weeks)
```
<p class="small muted">Read from the inside out. Nobody enjoys this.</p>
</div>
<div>
### With
```r
births |>
  select(infant_id, ga_weeks, site) |>
  filter(ga_weeks < 37) |>
  arrange(ga_weeks)
```
<p class="small muted">"Take births, <b>then</b> select, <b>then</b> filter, <b>then</b> sort."</p>
</div>
:::

::: {.small .muted}
<kbd>Ctrl</kbd>/<kbd>Cmd</kbd> + <kbd>Shift</kbd> + <kbd>M</kbd> inserts a pipe in RStudio.
You'll also see `%>%` from `magrittr` in older code — they behave the same for our purposes.
:::

---

## Verb 1–2: `filter()` and `select()` {.smaller}

`filter()` picks **rows**. `select()` picks **columns**.

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| min-lines: 8
births |>
  filter(ga_weeks < 37, site == "Ottawa") |>      # commas mean AND
  select(infant_id, ga_weeks, birth_weight_g, sex) |>
  arrange(ga_weeks)
```

::: {.rs .smaller}
<div class="r-side">
<h4>R</h4>

```r
filter(ga_weeks < 37)
select(id, ga_weeks)
```
</div>
<div class="sas-side">
<h4>SAS</h4>

```sas
IF ga_weeks < 37;
KEEP id ga_weeks;
```
</div>
:::

---

## Verb 3: `mutate()` — deriving variables {.smaller}

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| min-lines: 10
births2 <- births |>
  mutate(
    sex      = toupper(sex),                       # fix F/f/M/m
    bw_kg    = birth_weight_g / 1000,
    preterm  = ga_weeks < 37,                      # logical: TRUE/FALSE
    ga_group = case_when(
      ga_weeks < 32            ~ "very preterm",
      ga_weeks < 37            ~ "preterm",
      ga_weeks < 42            ~ "term",
      .default                 = "post-term"
    ),
    ga_group = factor(ga_group,
                      levels = c("term", "preterm", "very preterm", "post-term"))
  )

count(births2, ga_group)
```

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple" .smaller}
`case_when()` evaluates **top to bottom and stops at the first match** — exactly like a
SAS `IF/ELSE IF` chain. Order your conditions from most specific to least.
:::

---

## Your turn: derive and categorise {.smaller}

Create a birth-weight category and count it.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_mutate
#| min-lines: 10
births |>
  mutate(
    bw_cat = case_when(
      birth_weight_g < 1500 ~ "very low",
      birth_weight_g < ______ ~ "low",
      .default = "normal"
    )
  ) |>
  ______(bw_cat)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_mutate"}
<h4>Hint</h4>

The conventional low-birth-weight cut-point is 2500 g. To tabulate a variable in `dplyr`,
the verb is `count()`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_mutate"}
<h4>Solution</h4>

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_mutate
#| solution: true
births |>
  mutate(
    bw_cat = case_when(
      birth_weight_g < 1500 ~ "very low",
      birth_weight_g < 2500 ~ "low",
      .default = "normal"
    )
  ) |>
  count(bw_cat)
```
:::

---

## Verbs 4–5: `group_by()` + `summarise()` {.smaller}

This pair replaces `PROC MEANS` / `PROC SUMMARY` and does far more.

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| min-lines: 9
births |>
  mutate(sex = toupper(sex)) |>
  group_by(site, sex) |>
  summarise(
    n         = n(),
    mean_bw   = mean(birth_weight_g),
    sd_bw     = sd(birth_weight_g),
    pct_preterm = 100 * mean(ga_weeks < 37),
    .groups   = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(n))
```

::: {.small .muted}
`.groups = "drop"` un-groups the result. Forget it and every later verb silently operates
within group — a subtle and very common bug.
:::

---

## Your turn: group and summarise {.smaller}

Mean and SD of gestational age, by delivery mode, with the number in each group.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_group
#| min-lines: 9
births |>
  ______(delivery_mode) |>
  summarise(
    n       = ______,
    mean_ga = mean(ga_weeks),
    sd_ga   = ______(ga_weeks),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_group"}
<h4>Hint</h4>

The grouping verb is `group_by()`. `n()` counts rows in the current group (no arguments).
`sd()` is the standard deviation.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_group"}
<h4>Solution</h4>

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_group
#| solution: true
births |>
  group_by(delivery_mode) |>
  summarise(
    n       = n(),
    mean_ga = mean(ga_weeks),
    sd_ga   = sd(ga_weeks),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```
:::


# Joins {.section-break background-color="#8b1d41"}

## The four joins you need {.smaller}

::: {.cols}
<div>
```r
left_join(a, b, by = "id")
```
<p class="small">Keep <b>all of a</b>. Unmatched rows of a get <code>NA</code>.
<b>This is your default.</b> It preserves your cohort.</p>

```r
inner_join(a, b, by = "id")
```
<p class="small">Keep only rows present in <b>both</b>. Silently drops cases —
so always know how many.</p>
</div>
<div>
```r
full_join(a, b, by = "id")
```
<p class="small">Keep everything from both. Useful when assembling a cohort from
multiple registries.</p>

```r
anti_join(a, b, by = "id")
```
<p class="small">Rows of a with <b>no</b> match in b. <b>An auditing tool</b> —
"who is missing a screening result, and are they different?"</p>
</div>
:::

::: {.rs .smaller}
<div class="r-side">
<h4>R</h4>

```r
left_join(births, mothers, by = "momid")
```
</div>
<div class="sas-side">
<h4>SAS</h4>

```sas
DATA out; MERGE births(IN=a) mothers;
  BY momid; IF a; RUN;
```
</div>
:::

---

## The join that ruins analyses [live]{.time} {.smaller}

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| min-lines: 7
nrow(births)                                          # 1239 infants

naive <- left_join(births, screening, by = "infant_id")
nrow(naive)                                           # …and now?

# where did the extra rows come from?
naive |> count(infant_id) |> filter(n > 1) |> head(4)
```

. . .

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
**Your cohort just grew by 133 rows.** 133 infants had a repeat screening specimen, so each of them now
contributes **two rows**. Every subsequent `n()`, mean, and regression is now weighted
towards infants who were screened twice — which is to say, towards the sickest infants.
Nothing errored. Nothing warned you.
:::

---

## Fix it: decide *which* record you want {.smaller}

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| min-lines: 10
# Option A — keep the first (initial) specimen only. Usually what you want.
first_spec <- screening |>
  filter(specimen_no == 1)

# Option B — keep the earliest collection per infant, whatever it's numbered
first_spec_b <- screening |>
  group_by(infant_id) |>
  slice_min(age_at_collection_h, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup()

cohort <- births |> left_join(first_spec, by = "infant_id")

c(births = nrow(births), cohort = nrow(cohort))       # now they match
```

::: {.keypoint .smaller}
**The habit that will save you:** print `nrow()` before and after every join.
If the number changed and you didn't expect it to, stop.
:::

---

## `anti_join()` — who did we lose, and are they different? {.smaller}

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| min-lines: 8
unscreened <- anti_join(births, screening, by = "infant_id")
nrow(unscreened)

# Never just drop them. Compare them first.
bind_rows(
  unscreened |> mutate(grp = "no screen"),
  semi_join(births, screening, by = "infant_id") |> mutate(grp = "screened")
) |>
  group_by(grp) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_ga = mean(ga_weeks), mean_bw = mean(birth_weight_g))
```

::: {.small .muted}
If the unmatched infants are systematically smaller or earlier, your complete-case analysis
is biased and you need to say so. This three-line check belongs in every linkage paper you write.
:::

---

## One more trap: many-to-one on the *mother* {.smaller}

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| min-lines: 7
nrow(births); nrow(mothers)

full <- cohort |> left_join(mothers, by = "momid")
nrow(full)                                    # unchanged — good

# but note: mothers of twins are counted twice at the infant level
full |> count(momid) |> filter(n > 1) |> nrow()
```

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" .smaller}
That is **not** a bug — an infant-level analysis correctly has one row per infant.
But those infants are **not independent**, so a standard `glm()` understates the standard
errors. You would need a cluster-robust variance or a random effect for `momid`.
Recognising the clustering is the epidemiology; the join is just plumbing.
:::

---

## Your turn: build the analysis cohort {.smaller}

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_join
#| min-lines: 10
analysis <- births |>
  mutate(sex = toupper(sex)) |>
  left_join(screening |> filter(specimen_no ______ 1), by = "infant_id") |>
  ______(mothers, by = "momid")

# it MUST still have 1239 rows
nrow(analysis)
nrow(analysis) == nrow(births)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_join"}
<h4>Hint</h4>

You want only the *first* specimen, so `specimen_no` should equal 1 (`==`).
For the second join you want to keep every infant, so use `left_join()`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_join"}
<h4>Solution</h4>

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_join
#| solution: true
analysis <- births |>
  mutate(sex = toupper(sex)) |>
  left_join(screening |> filter(specimen_no == 1), by = "infant_id") |>
  left_join(mothers, by = "momid")

nrow(analysis)
nrow(analysis) == nrow(births)
```
:::


# Dates, missingness, shape {.section-break}

## Dates with `lubridate` {.smaller}

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| min-lines: 10
class(births$birth_datetime)          # read_csv already recognised this as a datetime

d <- births |>
  mutate(
    birth_date  = as_date(birth_datetime),
    birth_month = month(birth_datetime, label = TRUE),
    birth_wday  = wday(birth_datetime, label = TRUE),
    ga_days     = round(ga_weeks * 7)
  )

count(d, birth_wday)
```

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" .smaller}
`read_csv()` parses ISO-style datetimes for you; `read.csv()` leaves them as text.
When a date arrives as text — and from SAS or Excel it usually does — parse it explicitly
with the function whose **name is the format**: `ymd()`, `dmy()`, `ymd_hm()`, `mdy_hms()`.
:::

---

## Date arithmetic: time to specimen collection {.smaller}

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| min-lines: 10
timing <- births |>
  select(infant_id, birth_datetime) |>
  left_join(select(screening, infant_id, specimen_no, collection_datetime),
            by = "infant_id") |>
  mutate(
    hours_to_collection = as.numeric(difftime(collection_datetime, birth_datetime,
                                              units = "hours")),
    too_early = hours_to_collection < 24          # screening guideline flag
  )

timing |> group_by(specimen_no) |>
  summarise(n = n(), median_h = median(hours_to_collection), n_early = sum(too_early))
```

::: {.rs .smaller}
<div class="r-side">
<h4>R</h4>

```r
as_date(x); year(x); month(x, label = TRUE)
difftime(b, a, units = "hours")
```
</div>
<div class="sas-side">
<h4>SAS</h4>

```sas
dob = DATEPART(birth_dtm);
FORMAT dob date9.;
hrs = INTCK('hour', birth_dtm, coll_dtm);
```
</div>
:::

---

## Missing data — think, then act {.smaller}

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| min-lines: 9
analysis <- births |>
  mutate(sex = toupper(sex)) |>
  left_join(filter(screening, specimen_no == 1), by = "infant_id") |>
  left_join(mothers, by = "momid")

# how much, and where?
analysis |> summarise(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.x)))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "var", values_to = "n_missing") |>
  filter(n_missing > 0)
```

::: {.keypoint .smaller}
`drop_na()` is one keystroke and a substantive decision. Complete-case analysis is only
unbiased under **MCAR** — a strong assumption you should state and, ideally, test.
For anything going in a paper, look at `mice` for multiple imputation.
:::

---

## Wide → long with `pivot_longer()` {.smaller}

Five analytes in five columns is convenient for storage and useless for plotting.

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| min-lines: 9
long <- analysis |>
  select(infant_id, ga_weeks, tsh, x17ohp, phe, leu, ala) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = c(tsh, x17ohp, phe, leu, ala),
    names_to  = "analyte",
    values_to = "value"
  )

long |> group_by(analyte) |>
  summarise(n = sum(!is.na(value)), median = median(value, na.rm = TRUE))
```

::: {.small .muted}
`pivot_wider()` goes the other way. In SAS this is `PROC TRANSPOSE`, which is —
and this is a defensible professional opinion — considerably less pleasant.
:::

---

## A publishable "Table 1" {.smaller}

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| min-lines: 11
analysis |>
  mutate(preterm = if_else(ga_weeks < 37, "Preterm (<37wk)", "Term")) |>
  group_by(preterm) |>
  summarise(
    n            = n(),
    `Mat. age`   = sprintf("%.1f (%.1f)", mean(mat_age), sd(mat_age)),
    `Mat. BMI`   = sprintf("%.1f (%.1f)", mean(mat_bmi, na.rm = TRUE), sd(mat_bmi, na.rm = TRUE)),
    `Smoking %`  = sprintf("%.1f", 100 * mean(smoking == "yes")),
    `Hypert. %`  = sprintf("%.1f", 100 * mean(hypertension)),
    `Birth wt g` = sprintf("%.0f (%.0f)", mean(birth_weight_g), sd(birth_weight_g)),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" .smaller}
In RStudio, `gtsummary::tbl_summary(data, by = preterm) |> add_p()` does all of this —
with formatting, p-values, and export to Word — in two lines. Try it locally:
`install.packages("gtsummary")`.
:::


# Visualisation {.section-break}

## The grammar of graphics {.smaller}

Every `ggplot` is the same three things: **data**, an **aesthetic mapping**
(which variable goes on which channel), and one or more **geoms**.

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| min-lines: 6
ggplot(analysis, aes(x = ga_weeks)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5, fill = "#8b1d41", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 37, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.9, colour = "#12707a") +
  labs(title = "Gestational age at birth", x = "Completed weeks", y = "Infants")
```

---

## Comparing groups {.smaller}

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| min-lines: 6
analysis |>
  filter(!is.na(sex)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = site, y = birth_weight_g, fill = sex)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.alpha = 0.4) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Birth weight (g)", fill = "Sex",
       title = "Birth weight by site and sex")
```

---

## The plot that answers our question {.smaller}

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| min-lines: 8
analysis |>
  filter(!is.na(x17ohp)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = ga_weeks, y = x17ohp)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.45, colour = "#21303b") +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = TRUE, colour = "#8b1d41") +
  scale_y_log10(labels = label_number()) +
  labs(x = "Gestational age (weeks)", y = "17-OHP (nmol/L, log scale)",
       title = "17-OHP falls steeply with increasing gestational age")
```

::: {.small .muted}
`scale_y_log10()` is doing real work here — 17-OHP is strongly right-skewed, which is why
newborn screening programmes use **gestational-age-stratified cut-points** rather than one
threshold for everyone.
:::

---

## Your turn: faceting {.smaller}

Split the birth-weight-by-gestational-age relationship by sex.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_plot
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.2
#| min-lines: 8
analysis |>
  filter(!is.na(sex)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = ga_weeks, y = birth_weight_g)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  ______(~ sex) +
  labs(x = "Gestational age (weeks)", y = "Birth weight (g)")
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_plot"}
<h4>Hint</h4>

The function that splits a plot into panels by one variable is `facet_wrap()`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_plot"}
<h4>Solution</h4>

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_plot
#| solution: true
analysis |>
  filter(!is.na(sex)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = ga_weeks, y = birth_weight_g)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  facet_wrap(~ sex) +
  labs(x = "Gestational age (weeks)", y = "Birth weight (g)")
```
:::


# Modelling {.section-break}

## Linear and logistic, and `broom` {.smaller}

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| min-lines: 10
m1 <- lm(birth_weight_g ~ ga_weeks + sex + smoking + mat_age, data = analysis)
tidy(m1, conf.int = TRUE) |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2)))

m2 <- glm(I(ga_weeks < 37) ~ mat_age + smoking + hypertension + diabetes_pre,
          data = analysis, family = binomial)

tidy(m2, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3)))
```

::: {.keypoint .smaller}
`broom::tidy()` turns any model into a **data frame** — so odds ratios and CIs flow straight
into `ggplot()`, `knitr::kable()`, or a `.csv` for your manuscript. No more copying numbers
out of printed output by hand. That alone is worth the switch from SAS.
:::

---

## Checking the model, and the R ↔ SAS map {.smaller}

::: {.cols}
<div>
```r
glance(m1)          # R², AIC, F, df
augment(m1)         # fitted values + residuals
par(mfrow = c(2,2)); plot(m1)
```
<p class="small"><code>augment()</code> gives you residuals as a column, so diagnostics
are just another ggplot.</p>
</div>
<div>
| R | SAS |
|---|---|
| `lm()` | `PROC REG` / `GLM` |
| `glm(family=binomial)` | `PROC LOGISTIC` |
| `glm(family=poisson)` | `PROC GENMOD` |
| `coxph(Surv(t,d)~x)` | `PROC PHREG` |
| `lme4::lmer()` | `PROC MIXED` |
| `survey::svyglm()` | `PROC SURVEYLOGISTIC` |
</div>
:::


# AI coding assistants {.section-break background-color="#8b1d41"}

## What we're talking about [15 min]{.time} {.smaller}

| | Examples | Where it lives |
|---|---|---|
| **Chat assistants** | Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini | Browser. You paste code in and out. |
| **In-editor completion** | GitHub Copilot, Positron Assistant, RStudio + `chattr`/`ellmer` | Suggests as you type, sees your open files |
| **Agentic tools** | Claude Code, Codex, Cursor | Reads *and writes* files, runs code, iterates |
| **Institution-hosted** | Azure OpenAI / Bedrock behind a hospital firewall | Same models, data stays inside the tenancy |

: {tbl-colwidths="[24,40,36]"}

. . .

::: {.keypoint .smaller}
These are now ordinary tools for research programming, and pretending otherwise does not
serve you. But they are **assistants**, not analysts — the last two rows of this table are
also where the data-governance questions get serious.
:::

---

## What they are genuinely good at {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
- **Translating between languages.** "Here is a SAS `PROC LOGISTIC` with a `CLASS` statement — write the R equivalent." This works remarkably well and is worth knowing about on day one.
- **Boilerplate and syntax you'd otherwise look up.** `ggplot` theming, `regex`, reshaping, date parsing, `case_when` chains.
- **Explaining code you inherited.** "What does this 200-line DATA step actually do?" — then *you* verify.
- **Decoding error messages.** Paste the error and the offending line; you'll usually get a real answer faster than a search.
- **Writing comments and documentation** for code you already wrote and understand.
- **Being a rubber duck at 11pm** when your supervisor is asleep.
:::

---

## The hard rules for health data {.smaller}

::: {.keypoint}
**Nothing that identifies a person, and nothing from a secure analytic environment,
ever goes into a cloud AI tool. No exceptions, no "just this once", no "it's only 10 rows".**
:::

::: {.incremental .smaller}
- **No row-level data.** Not ICES, not BORN, not TOHDW, not your REB-approved chart abstraction. Pasting it is a privacy breach and likely a DUA violation, whether or not anything bad happens next.
- **Secure environments are secure environments.** If you cannot copy data out, you cannot copy data out *into a chat window* either. That includes screenshots.
- **Direct identifiers are obvious; indirect ones are not.** Postal code + birth date + rare diagnosis re-identifies a person as surely as a name.
- **Your DUA and REB protocol govern.** Read the data-sharing clause. Ask your data custodian *before*, not after.
- **Check your institution's policy.** uOttawa, OHRI, CHEO and ICES each have one, and they differ.
:::

---

## How to work safely anyway {.smaller}

::: {.cols}
<div>
### Send the *schema*, never the data
```r
# paste THIS, not the dataset
str(analysis)
# or an obviously fake sample:
head(analysis) |>
  mutate(across(everything(),
                ~ sample(.x)))
```
<p class="small">The model needs column names and types to write correct code.
It does not need your patients.</p>
</div>
<div>
### Develop on synthetic data
<p class="small">Write and debug against simulated data that has the same structure
(exactly like the files we used today), then move the finished script into the secure
environment and run it there. This is how a lot of professional analytic work is actually
done, and it is a defensible workflow to describe in a methods section.</p>
</div>
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" .smaller}
**Ask about an institution-hosted option.** Many hospitals and universities now run models
inside their own tenancy where data does not leave the boundary. That changes the calculus —
but confirm it in writing, don't assume it from a vendor's marketing page.
:::

---

## Prompting for code you can actually use {.smaller}

::: {.cols-40-60}
<div>
### Weak
```text
make me a graph of birth weight
```
</div>
<div>
### Strong
```text
I have a data frame `analysis` (1239 rows):
ga_weeks (num), birth_weight_g (int),
sex (chr "M"/"F"), site (chr, 5 levels).

Write tidyverse/ggplot2 code for a scatter
plot of birth weight vs gestational age,
faceted by sex, with a linear smooth and
95% CI. Label axes for a journal figure.
Comment each step. R 4.4, ggplot2 3.5.
```
</div>
:::

::: {.incremental .smaller}
- **State the dialect** — "tidyverse", "base R", "data.table". Otherwise you get a mash of all three.
- **Give the schema and the row count.** Column names and types are what it actually needs.
- **Ask for comments**, then read them. If a comment doesn't match the code, the code is wrong.
- **Ask it to explain its choice** of test/model. A vague justification is a red flag.
- **Iterate.** "That dropped the NAs silently — rewrite it so missingness is explicit."
:::

---

## The hallucination trap {.smaller}

These models are trained to produce **plausible** text. Plausible R code that runs and
returns a number is the most dangerous possible failure mode, because nothing alerts you.

::: {.incremental .smaller}
- **Invented functions and arguments.** `tidyverse::clean_names()`, `geom_boxplot(se = TRUE)`, a `conf.level` argument that doesn't exist. These at least error.
- **Wrong defaults, silently.** `mean()` without `na.rm`. `cor()` dropping pairs. `type = "response"` omitted from `predict()`.
- **Statistically wrong but syntactically perfect.** A `gaussian` family on a binary outcome. A t-test on paired data. Ignoring clustering by mother. It runs. It prints. It's wrong.
- **Confidently wrong citations and package claims.** It will tell you a package does something it does not.
- **Sycophancy.** Push back on a correct answer and it will often "correct" itself into an error.
:::

. . .

::: {.keypoint .smaller}
**You are the author.** Your name goes on the paper; the model's does not.
Treat generated code exactly as you would code from a fast, confident, well-read
summer student who has never once said "I'm not sure".
:::

---

## Live exercise: spot the bugs [8 min]{.time} {.smaller}

I asked an assistant for "the analysis of preterm birth". It produced this. **It runs.**
There are **four** things wrong with it. Find them, then fix them.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_bug
#| min-lines: 14
cohort <- births |>
  left_join(screening, by = "infant_id") |>
  left_join(mothers,   by = "momid")

cohort |> summarise(
  n           = n(),
  mean_bw     = mean(birth_weight_g),
  mean_17ohp  = mean(x17ohp)
)

count(cohort, sex)

m <- glm(I(ga_weeks < 37) ~ mat_age + smoking + mat_bmi,
         data = cohort, family = gaussian)
tidy(m, exponentiate = TRUE)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_bug"}
<h4>Hint</h4>

1. Compare `nrow(cohort)` with `nrow(births)`. Which join changed the row count, and why?
2. Look at `mean_17ohp`. Why is it `NA`?
3. Look at the output of `count(cohort, sex)`. How many sexes are there?
4. `ga_weeks < 37` is TRUE/FALSE. Is `gaussian` the right family for that — and does
   `exponentiate = TRUE` mean anything if it isn't?
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_bug"}
<h4>Solution</h4>

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_bug
#| solution: true
# 1. Keep ONE screening record per infant, or the cohort inflates 1239 -> 1372
# 2. mean() needs na.rm = TRUE; 17-OHP has missing values
# 3. sex is coded F/M/f/m and must be harmonised before it is used
# 4. A binary outcome needs family = binomial; only then does exponentiate = TRUE
#    give odds ratios rather than nonsense
cohort <- births |>
  mutate(sex = toupper(sex)) |>
  left_join(filter(screening, specimen_no == 1), by = "infant_id") |>
  left_join(mothers, by = "momid")

stopifnot(nrow(cohort) == nrow(births))     # guard rail: fail loudly

cohort |> summarise(
  n          = n(),
  mean_bw    = mean(birth_weight_g, na.rm = TRUE),
  mean_17ohp = mean(x17ohp, na.rm = TRUE),
  n_missing_17ohp = sum(is.na(x17ohp))
)

count(cohort, sex)

m <- glm(I(ga_weeks < 37) ~ mat_age + smoking + mat_bmi,
         data = cohort, family = binomial)
tidy(m, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)
# (and note: twins mean rows are clustered within momid — a robust or
#  mixed-effects variance would be more honest still)
```
:::

---

## A workable policy for your thesis {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
1. **Never** paste real data, output containing small cells, or anything from a secure environment.
2. Use it freely for **syntax, translation, explanation, and debugging**.
3. **Run every line yourself** and check the intermediate objects — `nrow()`, `count()`, `summary()`.
4. Never accept a **statistical choice** you couldn't defend in your comprehensive exam.
5. **Keep the code in version control** so you can see what changed and when.
6. **Disclose it** if your journal, funder, or program asks — and increasingly they do.
:::

. . .

::: {.keypoint .smaller}
The skill that matters is no longer typing `ggplot` from memory. It is **knowing when the
answer is wrong** — and that still comes from understanding your data and your methods.
That is what this degree is for.
:::
